Take the top row first, in full. An S&P 500 ETF at $500 quoted a penny wide: the spread is $0.01 ÷ $500 × 10,000 = 0.2 bps, and that is also what the round trip costs. It moves about 1 per cent on an average day, which is 100 bps. So the friction ratio is 0.2 ÷ 100, or 0.2 per cent, and 99.8 per cent of the day’s movement is still there for you to be right or wrong about.

Now the bottom row. A $1.50 micro-cap quoted five cents wide: $0.05 ÷ $1.50 × 10,000 = 333 bps for the round trip. It moves about 9 per cent on an average day, which is 900 bps. The ratio is 333 ÷ 900, or 37 per cent.

Read the bottom row once more as a requirement rather than a cost. At 37 per cent you must be right about more than a third of the day’s entire movement before you have covered the price of showing up. No edge in this course survives that. The micro-cap is not a harder version of the same game.
